claim: Alpha-synuclein (α-syn) is a major component of Lewy bodies found in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients.
source: Alpha-synuclein (α-syn), a major component of Lewy bodies found in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients, has been found exported outside of cells and may mediate its toxicity via cell-to-cell transmission.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: α-syn has been found exported outside of cells.
source: Alpha-synuclein (α-syn), a major component of Lewy bodies found in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients, has been found exported outside of cells and may mediate its toxicity via cell-to-cell transmission.
evidence: This statement is supported by the literature and the experimental work presented in the manuscript.

claim: α-syn may mediate its toxicity via cell-to-cell transmission.
source: Alpha-synuclein (α-syn), a major component of Lewy bodies found in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients, has been found exported outside of cells and may mediate its toxicity via cell-to-cell transmission.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by various studies cited in the introduction.

claim: Soluble, monomeric α-syn secretion can be reconstituted by the expression of DNAJC5 in HEK293T cells.
source: Here, we reconstituted soluble, monomeric α-syn secretion by the expression of DnaJ homolog subfamily C member 5 (DNAJC5) in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, demonstrated through experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: DNAJC5 undergoes palmitoylation and anchors on the membrane.
source: DNAJC5 undergoes palmitoylation and anchors on the membrane.
evidence: This is demonstrated through cellular fractionation and depalmitoylation assays shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Palmitoylation is essential for DNAJC5-induced α-syn secretion.
source: Palmitoylation is essential for DNAJC5-induced α-syn secretion, and the secretion is not limited by substrate size or unfolding.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using palmitoylation inhibitors and palmitoylation-deficient mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: α-syn secretion is not limited by substrate size or unfolding.
source: Palmitoylation is essential for DNAJC5-induced α-syn secretion, and the secretion is not limited by substrate size or unfolding.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with α-syn tandem repeats and folded protein fusions shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cytosolic α-syn is actively translocated and sequestered in an endosomal membrane compartment in a DNAJC5-dependent manner.
source: Cytosolic α-syn is actively translocated and sequestered in an endosomal membrane compartment in a DNAJC5-dependent manner.
evidence: This is shown through live-cell imaging and protease protection assays in Figure 4.

claim: Reduction of α-syn secretion caused by a palmitoylation-deficient mutation in DNAJC5 can be reversed by a membrane-targeting peptide fusion-induced oligomerization of DNAJC5.
source: Reduction of α-syn secretion caused by a palmitoylation-deficient mutation in DNAJC5 can be reversed by a membrane-targeting peptide fusion-induced oligomerization of DNAJC5.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with XPACK-DNAJC5 fusions shown in Figure 6.

claim: The secretion of endogenous α-syn mediated by DNAJC5 is found in a human neuroblastoma cell line, SH-SY5Y, differentiated into neurons in the presence of retinoic acid.
source: The secretion of endogenous α-syn mediated by DNAJC5 is also found in a human neuroblastoma cell line, SH-SY5Y, differentiated into neurons in the presence of retinoic acid, and in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived midbrain dopamine neurons.
evidence: This is shown through ELISA and knockdown experiments in Figure 7.

claim: The secretion of endogenous α-syn mediated by DNAJC5 is found in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived midbrain dopamine neurons.
source: The secretion of endogenous α-syn mediated by DNAJC5 is also found in a human neuroblastoma cell line, SH-SY5Y, differentiated into neurons in the presence of retinoic acid, and in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived midbrain dopamine neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with hiPSC-derived dopamine neurons shown in Figure 7.

claim: DNAJC5 forms a palmitoylated oligomer to accommodate and export α-syn.
source: We propose that DNAJC5 forms a palmitoylated oligomer to accommodate and export α-syn.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings, particularly the oligomerization data in Figure 6 and the rescue experiments with XPACK fusions.

claim: Parkinson's disease is the second most common neurodegenerative disease.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most common neurodegenerative disease, is characterized by the deposit of clumps of protein aggregate, lipid and damaged organelles known as Lewy bodies (LBs) (Dauer and Przedborski, 2003; Shahmoradian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a well-known fact in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Parkinson's disease is characterized by the deposit of clumps of protein aggregate, lipid and damaged organelles known as Lewy bodies.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most common neurodegenerative disease, is characterized by the deposit of clumps of protein aggregate, lipid and damaged organelles known as Lewy bodies (LBs) (Dauer and Przedborski, 2003; Shahmoradian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of PD, supported by citations.

claim: One of the main constituents of Lewy bodies is the presynaptic protein alpha-synuclein (α-syn).
source: One of the main constituents of LB is the presynaptic protein alpha-synuclein (α-syn) (Stefanis, 2012).
evidence: This is a well-known fact supported by citation.

claim: α-syn is encoded by the SNCA gene.
source: α-syn is encoded by the SNCA gene and is highly abundant in neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: α-syn is highly abundant in neurons.
source: α-syn is encoded by the SNCA gene and is highly abundant in neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: α-syn is a small, intrinsically disordered protein containing 140 amino acids.
source: As a small, intrinsically disordered protein-containing 140 amino acids (AAs), α-syn can be divided into three domains, an amphipathic N-terminal domain where most PD-related mutations are located, including A30P, E46K, and A53T, a central hydrophobic region known as the non-amyloid-β component (NAC) which is essential for aggregation, and an acidic C-terminal domain (Figure 1A; Alderson and Markley, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: α-syn can be divided into three domains: an amphipathic N-terminal domain, a central hydrophobic region known as the non-amyloid-β component (NAC), and an acidic C-terminal domain.
source: As a small, intrinsically disordered protein-containing 140 amino acids (AAs), α-syn can be divided into three domains, an amphipathic N-terminal domain where most PD-related mutations are located, including A30P, E46K, and A53T, a central hydrophobic region known as the non-amyloid-β component (NAC) which is essential for aggregation, and an acidic C-terminal domain (Figure 1A; Alderson and Markley, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Most PD-related mutations in α-syn are located in the N-terminal domain, including A30P, E46K, and A53T.
source: As a small, intrinsically disordered protein-containing 140 amino acids (AAs), α-syn can be divided into three domains, an amphipathic N-terminal domain where most PD-related mutations are located, including A30P, E46K, and A53T, a central hydrophobic region known as the non-amyloid-β component (NAC) which is essential for aggregation, and an acidic C-terminal domain (Figure 1A; Alderson and Markley, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The NAC region of α-syn is essential for aggregation.
source: As a small, intrinsically disordered protein-containing 140 amino acids (AAs), α-syn can be divided into three domains, an amphipathic N-terminal domain where most PD-related mutations are located, including A30P, E46K, and A53T, a central hydrophobic region known as the non-amyloid-β component (NAC) which is essential for aggregation, and an acidic C-terminal domain (Figure 1A; Alderson and Markley, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: α-syn can undergo a conformational change from a disordered monomer to an oligomer.
source: α-syn can undergo a conformational change from a disordered monomer to an oligomer (Burré et al., 2014; Lashuel et al., 2002), which can further polymerize to form insoluble fibrils (Guerrero-Ferreira et al., 2019; Guerrero-Ferreira et al., 2018; Strohäker et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: α-syn oligomers can further polymerize to form insoluble fibrils.
source: α-syn can undergo a conformational change from a disordered monomer to an oligomer (Burré et al., 2014; Lashuel et al., 2002), which can further polymerize to form insoluble fibrils (Guerrero-Ferreira et al., 2019; Guerrero-Ferreira et al., 2018; Strohäker et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Grafted neurons in PD patients developed α-syn positive Lewy bodies years after surgery, suggesting host-to-graft pathology propagation.
source: Grafted neurons in PD patients developed α-syn positive LBs years after surgery, suggesting host-to-graft pathology propagation (Kordower et al., 2008; Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that observed this phenomenon.

claim: The Braak hypothesis posits that α-syn aggregates can spread in a stereotyped manner from the gastrointestinal tract to the brain, causing neuron loss beginning in the brainstem, extending to the midbrain, and finally to the cortex.
source: Based on analysis of human pathology, the Braak hypothesis posits that α-syn aggregates can spread in a stereotyped manner from the gastrointestinal tract to the brain, causing neuron loss beginning in the brainstem, extending to the midbrain, and finally to the cortex (Braak et al., 2006; Braak et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a well-known hypothesis in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Braak-like transmission of in vitro generated α-syn fibrils has been recapitulated in mice and non-human primates.
source: In more recent work, Braak-like transmission of in vitro generated α-syn fibrils has been recapitulated in mice and non-human primates (Chu et al., 2019; Chung et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2019; Luk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Several mechanisms have been proposed for both monomeric and aggregated α-syn export and transfer, including unconventional exocytosis, exosomes, and membrane nanotubes.
source: Several mechanisms have been proposed for both monomeric and aggregated α-syn export and transfer, including unconventional exocytosis (Jang et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2005), exosomes (Danzer et al., 2012; Emmanouilidou et al., 2010; Stykel et al., 2021), and membrane nanotubes (Abounit et al., 2016; Scheiblich et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to various studies proposing these mechanisms.

claim: The extracellular existence of both monomeric and oligomeric α-syn was confirmed in blood and cerebrospinal fluid.
source: The extracellular existence of both monomeric and oligomeric α-syn was confirmed in blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (Borghi et al., 2000; El-Agnaf et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that detected α-syn in these fluids.

claim: Packaging of different conformational forms of α-syn inside extracellular vesicles has been reported but requires further scrutiny to differentiate membrane vesicles from secreted sedimentable aggregates.
source: Packaging of different conformational forms of α-syn inside extracellular vesicles (EVs) has been reported but requires further vigorous scrutiny to differentiate membrane vesicles from secreted sedimentable aggregates (Brahic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging existing reports while noting the need for further investigation, supported by citation.

claim: DNAJC5 is a co-chaperone of HSC70.
source: DNAJC5, also known as cysteine string protein α (CSPα), is a co-chaperone of HSC70 and has been shown to control the extracellular release of many neurodegenerative disease proteins (Fontaine et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: DNAJC5 has been shown to control the extracellular release of many neurodegenerative disease proteins.
source: DNAJC5, also known as cysteine string protein α (CSPα), is a co-chaperone of HSC70 and has been shown to control the extracellular release of many neurodegenerative disease proteins (Fontaine et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study demonstrating this function.

claim: The process of unconventional traffic mediated by DNAJC5 has been termed misfolding-associated protein secretion (MAPS).
source: This process of unconventional traffic has been termed misfolding-associated protein secretion (MAPS) (Fontaine et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016) as opposed to conventional secretion initiated by an amino-terminal signal peptide required for secretory and membrane protein translocation into the endoplasmic reticulum (Zhang and Schekman, 2013).
evidence: This is a defined term in the field, supported by citations.

claim: DNAJC5 contains three domains: a common N-terminal J-domain, the cysteine-string (CS) central domain which is heavily palmitoylated and anchors the protein to late endosomes, and an overall disordered C-terminal domain.
source: DNAJC5 contains three domains—a common N-terminal J-domain conserved among DnaJ proteins, the cysteine-string (CS) central domain which is heavily palmitoylated and anchors the protein to late endosomes, and an overall disordered C-terminal domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Deletion of DNAJC5 in Drosophila and mice leads to a neurodegenerative phenotype and premature death.
source: Deletion of DNAJC5 in Drosophila and mice leads to a neurodegenerative phenotype and premature death, indicating that DNAJC5 plays a neuroprotective role in the brain (Zinsmaier, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study demonstrating this phenotype.

claim: DNAJC5 plays a neuroprotective role in the brain.
source: Deletion of DNAJC5 in Drosophila and mice leads to a neurodegenerative phenotype and premature death, indicating that DNAJC5 plays a neuroprotective role in the brain (Zinsmaier, 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the deletion phenotype and supported by citation.

claim: Transgenic expression of α-syn appears to rescue the neurodegeneration seen on depletion of DNAJC5.
source: Transgenic expression of α-syn appears to rescue the neurodegeneration seen on depletion of DNAJC5 (Chandra et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study demonstrating this rescue effect.

claim: Neuron-derived EVs contain DNAJC5.
source: A previous study also reported that neuron-derived EVs contain DNAJC5 (Deng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study that detected DNAJC5 in EVs.

claim: The mechanism by which DNAJC5 recognizes and translocates soluble α-syn into a membrane compartment for secretion remains elusive.
source: However, the mechanism by which DNAJC5 recognizes and translocates soluble α-syn into a membrane compartment for secretion remains elusive.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Palmitoylation and oligomerization of DNAJC5 play previously underappreciated roles in the regulation of α-syn secretion.
source: Using biochemical characterization and imaging of internalized α-syn in enlarged endosomes as a secretory intermediate, we found previously underappreciated roles of palmitoylation and oligomerization of DNAJC5 in the regulation of α-syn secretion.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: α-syn secretion can be stimulated by overexpressing DNAJC5.
source: Previous studies have shown that α-syn secretion can be stimulated by overexpressing DNAJC5 (Fontaine et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The CS domain of DNAJC5 plays a role in promoting stable membrane attachment based on its overall hydrophobicity and by enabling post-translational palmitoylation.
source: The CS domain of DNAJC5 plays a role in promoting stable membrane attachment based on its overall hydrophobicity and by enabling post-translational palmitoylation catalyzed by membrane-bound Asp-His-His-Cys (DHHC) family palmitoyltransferases (Greaves and Chamberlain, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Coomassie blue staining revealed two bands of low and high mobility on SDS-PAGE in the membrane and cytosolic fractions of DNAJC5, respectively.
source: Coomassie blue staining revealed two bands of low and high mobility on SDS-PAGE in the membrane and cytosolic fractions, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Similar migration profiles of palmitoylated (P-) and non-palmitoylated (NP-) DNAJC5 have been reported.
source: Similar migration profiles of pamitoylated (P-) and non-palmitoylated (NP-) DNAJC5 have been reported (Greaves et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: DNAJC5 in MDA-MB-231 and Hela cells appeared predominantly to be in a palmitoylated and membrane-associated form compared to DNAJC5 in HEK293T cells.
source: Compared to DNAJC5 in HEK293T cells, DNAJC5 in MDA-MB-231 and Hela cells appeared predominantly to be in a palmitoylated and membrane-associated form (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The mobility of P-DNAJC5 in the membrane fraction shifted to that of NP-DNAJC5 after an overnight depalmitoylation reaction with hydroxylamine.
source: The mobility of P-DNAJC5 in the membrane fraction shifted to that of NP-DNAJC5 after an overnight depalmitoylation reaction with hydroxylamine (HA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Membrane anchoring of DNAJC5 requires palmitoylation.
source: Thus, we confirm that membrane anchoring of DNAJC5 requires palmitoylation in our assay.
evidence: This is concluded from the depalmitoylation experiments.

claim: At 16 hours after transfection, similar basal-levels secretion of α-syn was detected in both DNAJC5-negative and -positive conditions.
source: At 16 hour (h) after transfection, we detected similar basal-levels secretion of α-syn in both DNAJC5-negative and -positive conditions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Two bands of DNAJC5 corresponding to P-DNAJC5 and NP-DNAJC5 were seen in the lysate at 16 hours after transfection, but only the P-DNAJC5 was secreted into the medium.
source: Two bands of DNAJC5 corresponding to P-DNAJC5 and NP-DNAJC5 were seen in the lysate, but only the P-DNAJC5 was secreted into the medium (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The stimulation of α-syn secretion by DNAJC5 became obvious at 36 hours after transfection.
source: The stimulation of α-syn secretion by DNAJC5 became obvious at a longer incubation time (36 h), and at this time point NP-DNAJC5 was also enriched in the medium (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At 36 hours after transfection, NP-DNAJC5 was also enriched in the medium.
source: The stimulation of α-syn secretion by DNAJC5 became obvious at a longer incubation time (36 h), and at this time point NP-DNAJC5 was also enriched in the medium (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The release of α-syn was not caused by cell death as little to undetected levels of cytoplasmic tubulin were found in the culture medium fraction.
source: The release of α-syn was not caused by cell death as little to undetected levels of cytoplasmic tubulin found in the culture medium fraction (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 1D and E to rule out cell death as a cause of α-syn release.

claim: Cell viability was not affected by transfection of different constructs, as shown by trypan blue staining.
source: Cell viability was not affected by transfection of different constructs, as shown by trypan blue staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Secretion of several PD-causing α-syn mutant proteins (A30P, E46K, and A53T) was induced to differing levels by expression of DNAJC5.
source: In addition to wild-type (WT) α-syn, secretion of several PD-causing α-syn mutant proteins (A30P, E46K, and A53T) was also induced to differing levels by expression of DNAJC5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: Stimulated secretion of Nluc-α-syn by overexpression of DNAJC5 was confirmed by immunoblot, indicating that Nluc-fusion did not impede α-syn secretion.
source: Stimulated secretion of Nluc-α-syn by overexpression of DNAJC5 was confirmed by immunoblot, indicating that Nluc-fusion did not impede α-syn secretion (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Without overexpression of DNAJC5, accumulation of Nluc-α-syn signal in the medium over time was observed.
source: Without overexpression of DNAJC5, we observed accumulation of Nluc-α-syn signal in the medium over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Quercetin is a plant-derived flavonoid that has previously been shown to inhibit DNAJC5-mediated trafficking of a bacterial toxin.
source: Quercetin is a plant-derived flavonoid that has previously been shown to inhibit DNAJC5-mediated trafficking of a bacterial toxin (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D; Deruelle et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study and the chemical structure is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Quercetin inhibited Nluc-α-syn secretion in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We found that quercetin also inhibited Nluc-α-syn secretion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), implying a role for endogenous DNAJC5 in α-syn secretion.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Quercetin inhibition of Nluc-α-syn secretion implies a role for endogenous DNAJC5 in α-syn secretion.
source: We found that quercetin also inhibited Nluc-α-syn secretion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), implying a role for endogenous DNAJC5 in α-syn secretion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the quercetin inhibition experiment.

claim: Bafilomycin A1 (BaFA1) is a lysosomal ATPase inhibitor that has been shown to stimulate α-syn secretion.
source: Balfilomycin A1 (BaFA1), a lysosomal ATPase inhibitor, has been shown to stimulate α-syn secretion (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G; Buratta et al., 2020; Fernandes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3G.

claim: BaFA1 is known to stimulate the fusion of lysosomes and multivesicular bodies at the cell surface with the secretion of lysosomal content and exosomes.
source: BaFA1 is also known to stimulate the fusion of lysosomes and multivesicular bodies at the cell surface with the secretion of lysosomal content and exosomes (Cashikar and Hanson, 2019; Hikita et al., 2018; Tapper and Sundler, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: BaFA1-stimulated α-syn secretion was confirmed in WT HEK293T cells but substantially reduced in DNAJC5 KO cells.
source: BaFA1-stimulated α-syn secretion was confirmed in WT HEK293T cells but substantially reduced in DNAJC5 KO cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3H.

claim: DNAJC5 is required for the secretion of α-syn from the endosome/lysosome and is enhanced by overexpression of DNAJC5.
source: Our results suggest that DNAJC5 is required for the secretion of α-syn from the endosome/lysosome and is enhanced by overexpression of DNAJC5.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BaFA1 and DNAJC5 KO experiments.

claim: DNAJC5 and α-syn co-secrete into the medium.
source: In our established assay, DNAJC5 and α-syn co-secrete into the medium (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Secreted α-syn has been reported to be encapsulated inside EVs.
source: Secreted α-syn has been reported to be encapsulated inside EVs (Danzer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: After serial differential centrifugation, α-syn and NP-DNAJC5 remained soluble.
source: After serial differential centrifugation, α-syn and NP-DNAJC5 remained soluble.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the medium fractionation experiment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: P-DNAJC5 co-sedimented with other EV markers after 100k×g centrifugation.
source: In comparison, P-DNAJC5 co-sedimented with other EV markers after 100k×g centrifugation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the medium fractionation experiment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Several PD-causing α-syn mutants all remained soluble in culture supernatant fractions after medium fractionation.
source: In addition to WT α-syn, we conducted medium fractionation with several PD-causing α-syn mutants and found they all remained soluble in culture supernatant fractions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: P-DNAJC5 equilibrated with other EV markers to the 10%/40% interface expected for buoyant EVs in a sucrose step gradient flotation.
source: P-DNAJC5 equilibrated with other EV markers to the 10%/40% interface expected for buoyant EVs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the sucrose gradient flotation experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The secreted α-syn induced by DNAJC5 is neither membrane bound nor in a sedimentable fibrillar form.
source: We conclude that the secreted α-syn induced by DNAJC5 is neither membrane bound nor in a sedimentable fibrillar form.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the medium fractionation and flotation experiments.

claim: Extracellular α-syn eluted from a gel filtration column at around 60% of the column volume, similar to the elution volume of purified monomeric α-syn.
source: Extracellular α-syn eluted from the column at around 60% of the column volume (Figure 2C), similar to the elution volume of purified monomeric α-syn (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3E, F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the gel filtration experiment shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Only FLAG-tagged α-syn was immuno-precipitated in a co-IP assay, suggesting no stable interaction between FLAG-tagged and non-tagged α-syn.
source: We found that only the FLAG-tagged α-syn was immuno-precipitated (Figure 2F), suggesting no stable interaction between the two species.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the co-IP experiment shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The gel filtration and IP assays reinforced the conclusion that α-syn is secreted as a monomer.
source: The gel filtration and IP assays reinforced our conclusion that α-syn is secreted as a monomer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gel filtration and co-IP experiments.

claim: Membrane targeting of DNAJC5 is dependent upon palmitoylation.
source: Membrane targeting of DNAJC5 is dependent upon palmitoylation (Greaves et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Two specific mutations, L115R and L116Δ in the CS domain of DNAJC5, cause adult-onset neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL).
source: Two specific mutations, L115R and L116Δ in the CS domain, cause adult-onset neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL), a type of neurodegenerative disorder (Benitez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: NCL mutations reduce the level of DNAJC5 palmitoylation and promote aggregation of the protein.
source: NCL mutations reduce the level of DNAJC5 palmitoylation and promote aggregation of the protein (Diez-Ardanuy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: DNAJC5 palmitoylation largely decreased in the L115R mutant or upon 2-BA treatment.
source: DNAJC5 palmitoylation largely decreased in the L115R mutant or upon 2-BA treatment.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: NP-DNAJC5 accumulated in the cytosol when palmitoylation was reduced by L115R mutation or 2-BA treatment.
source: Correspondingly, NP-DNAJC5 accumulated in the cytosol (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Upon 10 μM 2-BA treatment, α-syn and DNAJC5 secretion were abolished.
source: Upon 10 μM 2-BA treatment, α-syn and DNAJC5 secretion were abolished (Figure 3C, E, F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 3C, E, F.

claim: The efficacy of 2-BA was validated by the disappearance of the low-mobility band corresponding to P-DNAJC5 in the cell lysate.
source: The efficacy of the inhibitor was validated by the disappearance of the low-mobility band corresponding to P-DNAJC5 in the cell lysate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 2-BA inhibited DNAJC5 palmitoylation and α-syn secretion in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, 2-BA inhibited DNAJC5 palmitoylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E) and α-syn secretion in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C, D, E.

claim: α-syn secretion was reduced by the palmitoylation-deficient DNAJC5 (L115R) compared with DNAJC5 (WT).
source: Likewise, α-syn secretion was reduced by the palmitoylation-deficient DNAJC5 (L115R) compared with DNAJC5 (WT) (Figure 3G–J).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 3G–J.

claim: DNAJC5 has been proposed to function downstream of the deubiquitinase USP19 in the MAPS pathway.
source: DNAJC5 has been proposed to function downstream of the deubiquitinase USP19 in the MAPS pathway (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: DNAJC5 carrying either NCL mutation L115R or L116Δ had no palmitoylated protein band detected in the lysate and blocked USP19-stimulated α-syn secretion.
source: In agreement with the model, DNAJC5 carrying either NCL mutation L115R or L116Δ had no palmitoylated protein band detected in the lysate (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) and blocked USP19-stimulated α-syn secretion (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B, C.

claim: Palmitoylation is essential for DNAJC5 membrane association and function in stimulating α-syn secretion.
source: These results establish that palmitoylation is essential for DNAJC5 membrane association and function in stimulating α-syn secretion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 2-BA and L115R mutation experiments.

claim: A previous study reported an altered distribution of DNAJC5 mutant protein to the Golgi apparatus and cytosol.
source: A previous study reported an altered distribution of DNAJC5 mutant protein to the Golgi apparatus and cytosol (Nosková et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: WT DNAJC5 did not colocalize with the Golgi marker GM130, whereas both the L115R mutant and 2-BA treated WT cells partially retained DNAJC5 in puncta coincident with the Golgi marker GM130.
source: In confocal immunofluorescence (IF) images, we confirmed that WT DNAJC5 did not colocalize with the Golgi marker GM130, whereas both the L115R mutant and 2-BA treated WT cells partially retained DNAJC5 in puncta coincident with the Golgi marker GM130 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B, C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the IF experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B, C.

claim: α-syn secretion depends upon an appropriate subcellular organelle localization of DNAJC5.
source: We conclude that α-syn secretion depends upon an appropriate subcellular organelle localization of DNAJC5.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the IF experiments showing altered localization of DNAJC5 mutants.

claim: DNAJC5 has been reported under normal conditions to be associated with late endosomes.
source: DNAJC5 has been reported under normal conditions to be associated with late endosomes (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Colocalization between endogenous DNAJC5 and the late-endosomal marker CD63 was found using confocal IF.
source: Using confocal IF, we found colocalization between endogenous DNAJC5 and the late-endosomal marker CD63 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the IF experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CD63 localized to the lumen of enlarged endosomes labeled by mCherry-Rab5Q79L.
source: As a positive control, CD63 localized to the lumen of enlarged endosomes labeled by mCherry-Rab5Q79L (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both diffuse and punctate DNAJC5 localized to the lumen of enlarged endosomes.
source: Both diffuse and punctate DNAJC5 localized to the lumen of enlarged endosomes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the live-cell imaging experiment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The DNAJC5 L115R mutant became disperse in the cytosol, rather than being internalized into enlarged endosomes.
source: Unlike WT DNAJC5, the DNAJC5 L115R mutant became disperse in the cytosol, rather than being internalized into enlarged endosomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: mNG-fused α-syn showed diffuse localization in both the cytosol and nucleus but was completely excluded from enlarged endosomes in L115R mutant cells.
source: In contrast, mNeonGreen (mNG)-fused α-syn showed diffuse localization in both the cytosol and nucleus but was completely excluded from enlarged endosomes in L115R mutant cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The entry of α-syn into enlarged endosomes containing internalized DNAJC5 was observed, implying the translocation of α-syn into the membrane compartment required DNAJC5.
source: Notably, we observed the entry of α-syn into enlarged endosomes containing internalized DNAJC5, implying the translocation of α-syn into the membrane compartment required DNAJC5 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiment shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ratio of α-syn-containing endosomes in cells increased significantly with DNAJC5 overexpression.
source: The ratio of α-syn-containing endosomes in cells increased significantly with DNAJC5 overexpression (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the quantification shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The DNAJC5 L115R mutants failed to induce entry of α-syn into enlarged endosomes.
source: With no luminal localization inside enlarged endosomes, the DNAJC5 L115R mutants also failed to induce entry of α-syn into the same compartments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both DNAJC5 and α-syn were enriched in a 25k membrane pellet fraction.
source: Both DNAJC5 and α-syn were enriched in a 25k membrane pellet fraction (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cell fractionation experiment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: α-syn and DNAJC5 were partially resistant to digestion by proteinase K in the absence but not in the presence of Triton X-100, consistent with the conclusion that about half of the proteins were sequestered within membrane compartments.
source: In a protease protection assay with 25k sedimented membranes, we found that α-syn and DNAJC5 were partially resistant to digestion by proteinase K in the absence but not in the presence of Triton X-100 consistent with the conclusion that about half of the proteins were sequestered within membrane compartments (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the protease protection assay shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Visual inspection and quantification results are consistent with a membrane translocation role for DNAJC5 prior to α-syn secretion.
source: Our visual inspection and quantification results are consistent with a membrane translocation role for DNAJC5 prior to α-syn secretion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging and fractionation experiments.

claim: In SEC61-mediated co-translational translocation, substrates enter the SEC61 translocon in an unfolded state.
source: In SEC61-mediated co-translational translocation, substrates enter the SEC61 translocon in an unfolded state (Rapoport et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In THU and CMA, substrate unfolding is also required for translocation across the membrane.
source: In THU and CMA, substrate unfolding is also required for translocation across the membrane (Kaushik and Cuervo, 2018; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Unfolding and size is not a limiting factor for α-syn secretion.
source: In striking contrast, unfolding and size is not a limiting factor for α-syn secretion (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with α-syn tandem repeats and folded protein fusions shown in Figure 5.

claim: Studies have shown the import of folded proteins into the matrix of peroxisomes and through the nuclear pore.
source: As a precedent of translocation without unfolding, studies have shown the import of folded proteins into the matrix of peroxisomes and obviously through the nuclear pore (Kim and Hettema, 2015; Lin and Hoelz, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DNAJC5 forms a series of extremely stable oligomers, which may provide versatile adaptors to accommodate diverse misfolded or folded substrates with different dimensions.
source: DNAJC5 forms a series of extremely stable oligomers, which may provide versatile adaptors to accommodate diverse misfolded or folded substrates with different dimensions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the oligomerization data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The structure of DNAJC5 oligomers may shed light on the principle of this folding-independent translocation pathway.
source: The structure of DNAJC5 oligomers may shed light on the principle of this folding-independent translocation pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: α-syn tandem repeats could be secreted upon overexpression of DNAJC5.
source: We first determined that these α-syn tandem repeats could also be secreted upon overexpression of DNAJC5 (Figure 5B), indicating that DNAJC5 can accommodate α-syn of different sizes.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DNAJC5 can accommodate α-syn of different sizes.
source: We first determined that these α-syn tandem repeats could also be secreted upon overexpression of DNAJC5 (Figure 5B), indicating that DNAJC5 can accommodate α-syn of different sizes.
evidence: This is inferred from the secretion of α-syn tandem repeats.

claim: Secreted tandem repeats of α-syn were also soluble.
source: Fractionation of the growth medium showed that secreted tandem repeats were also soluble (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the medium fractionation experiment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A three helix-bundle protein (3H) designed in the lowest-energy arrangements displayed extreme thermodynamic stability and remained folded even in non-physiological denaturing conditions.
source: For example, a three helix-bundle protein (3H) designed in the lowest-energy arrangements displayed extreme thermodynamic stability and remained folded even in non-physiological denaturing conditions (Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mitochondrial protein import is dependent on protein unfolding.
source: Given that mitochondrial protein import is dependent on protein unfolding (Neupert, 1997), we tested the effect of 3H insertion on the import of mitochondrial matrix enzyme ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) (Horwich et al., 1985; Yano et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: pOTC-GFP was enriched in a mitochondria-containing particulate (P) fraction compared to non-tagged GFP.
source: pOTC-GFP was enriched in a mitochondria-containing particulate (P) fraction compared to non-tagged GFP.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the mitochondrial import assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: A construct in which 3H was inserted between the leader sequence and GFP resulted in 80% of the fusion protein retained in the soluble fraction.
source: However, a construct in which 3H was inserted between the leader sequence and GFP resulted in 80% of the fusion protein retained in the soluble fraction (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the mitochondrial import assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: About 80% of citrate synthase (CS), a known mitochondria matrix protein, was protected from proteinase K.
source: About 80% of citrate synthase (CS), a known mitochondria matrix protein, was protected from proteinase K.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the protease protection assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E, F.

claim: Neither the mitochondrial outer membrane protein Tom20 nor pOTC-3H-GFP was protected from proteinase K, suggesting 3H prevented the translocation of GFP into mitochondria.
source: In contrast, neither the mitochondrial outer membrane protein Tom20 nor pOTC-3H-GFP was protected, suggesting 3H prevented the translocation of GFP into mitochondria (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E, F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the protease protection assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E, F.

claim: α-syn fusion proteins with 3H fused to either the N- or C-terminus were expressed and secreted normally into the growth medium.
source: Using a similar approach, we fused 3H to either the N- or C-terminus of α-syn to impede the unfolding process (Figure 5D). These α-syn fusion proteins were expressed and secreted normally into the growth medium (Figure 5E&F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 5E&F.

claim: Protein unfolding is dispensable for α-syn secretion.
source: These data suggest that protein unfolding is dispensable for α-syn secretion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments with 3H-fused α-syn.

claim: DNAJC5 has been reported to have an intrinsic propensity to form SDS-resistant oligomers.
source: DNAJC5 has been reported to have an intrinsic propensity to form SDS-resistant oligomers (Zhang and Chandra, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Many diffuse, ladder-like bands that migrated more slowly than the two corresponding to P-DNAJC5 and NP-DNAJC5 were noticed in a whole gel immunoblot of extracellular DNAJC5, possibly higher molecular weight (HMW) oligomers.
source: In a whole gel immunoblot of extracellular DNAJC5, we noticed many diffuse, ladder-like bands that migrated more slowly than the two corresponding to P-DNAJC5 and NP-DNAJC5 (Figure 6A), possibly higher molecular weight (HMW) oligomers.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunoblot shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Apparent oligomerization of DNAJC5 became more obvious when the J domain was deleted.
source: This apparent oligomerization of DNAJC5 became more obvious when the J domain was deleted (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The migration of HMW-DNAJC5 was not altered in samples heated in the presence of a reducing agent.
source: The migration of HMW-DNAJC5 was not altered in samples heated in the presence of a reducing agent (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HMW-DNAJC5 fractionated according to its apparent size, forming a stair-like pattern on the DNAJC5 immunoblot.
source: HMW-DNAJC5 fractionated according to its apparent size, forming a stair-like pattern on the DNAJC5 immunoblot (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the gel filtration experiment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HMW-DNAJC5 chromatographed within the gel filtration column volume, consistent with discrete protein species rather than aggregates.
source: HMW-DNAJC5 chromatographed within the gel filtration column volume, consistent with discrete protein species rather than aggregates (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the gel filtration experiment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: These results suggest the presence of higher-order, SDS-resistant, non-disulfide-bonded DNAJC5 oligomers both in intracellular and extracellular fractions.
source: These results suggest the presence of higher-order, SDS-resistant, non-disulfide-bonded DNAJC5 oligomers both in intracellular and extracellular fractions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the oligomerization experiments.

claim: XPACK (XP) is a membrane-targeting peptide sequence used widely in studies of cargo loading into exosomes and delivery to target cells of choice.
source: XPACK (XP) is a membrane-targeting peptide sequence used widely in studies of cargo loading into exosomes and delivery to target cells of choice (Yim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The exosome loading process by XP is dependent on two lipidation reactions—myristoylation on the first glycine and palmitoylation on the second cysteine.
source: The exosome loading process by XP is also dependent on two lipidation reactions—myristoylation on the first glycine and palmitoylation on the second cysteine (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C; Zacharias et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: An N-terminal XP fusion (XP-WT) resulted in the expression of a species that migrated at the position of P-DNAJC5, in contrast to the two species representing P- and NP-DNAJC5 in the WT DNAJC5 sample.
source: An N-terminal XP fusion (XP-WT) resulted in the expression of a species that migrated at the position of P-DNAJC5, in contrast to the two species representing P- and NP-DNAJC5 in the WT DNAJC5 sample (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: XP-DNAJC5 was exclusively associated with the sedimentable membrane fraction.
source: Again in contrast to WT DNAJC5, XP-DNAJC5 was exclusively associated with the sedimentable membrane fraction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the fractionation experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: XP-mediated lipidation was highly efficient and possibly irreversible.
source: This suggested that XP-mediated lipidation was highly efficient and possibly irreversible.
evidence: This is inferred from the exclusive membrane association of XP-DNAJC5.

claim: Formation of the lower electrophoretic mobility and membrane-associated form of XP-DNAJC5 was blocked by 2-BA treatment, indicating XP lipidation included palmitoylation.
source: Formation of the lower electrophoretic mobility and membrane-associated form of XP-DNAJC5 was blocked by 2-BA treatment, indicating XP lipidation included palmitoylation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: XP fusion to the palmitoylation-deficient mutant of DNAJC5 (L115R) did not produce a species that migrated at the position of P-DNAJC5 but resulted in several less abundant species that migrated between the positions of NP- and P-DNAJC5.
source: XP fusion to the palmitoylation-deficient mutant of DNAJC5 (L115R) did not produce a species that migrated at the position of P-DNAJC5 but resulted in several less abundant species that migrated between the positions of NP- and P-DNAJC5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The DXP-DNAJC5 L115R species had the same mobility as NP-DNAJC5.
source: The DXP-DNAJC5 L115R species had the same mobility as NP-DNAJC5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: XP-L115R was highly enriched in the membrane fraction, likely as a result of XPACK-mediated lipidation.
source: We conducted cellular fractionation on lysates of cells expressing DNAJC5 XP-L115R. XP-L115R was highly enriched in the membrane fraction, likely as a result of XPACK-mediated lipidation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the fractionation experiment shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SDS-PAGE of XP-L115R released by detergent solubilization migrated slowly and remained near the top of the gel, suggesting XPACK-induced high-order oligomerization or aggregation.
source: SDS-PAGE of XP-L115R released by detergent solubilization migrated slowly and remained near the top of the gel, suggesting XPACK-induced high-order oligomerization or aggregation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 6C.

claim: α-syn secretion was stimulated by the expression of both DNAJC5 XP-L115R and WT DNAJC5.
source: In spite of the apparent difference between DNAJC5 XP-L115R and WT DNAJC5, α-syn secretion was stimulated by the expression of both species (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the secretion assay shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Treatment with the palmitoylation inhibitor 2-BA resulted in the formation of XP-L115R that migrated to a position similar to that of monomeric DNAJC5.
source: Treatment with the palmitoylation inhibitor 2-BA resulted in the formation of XP-L115R that migrated to a position similar to that of monomeric DNAJC5 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Secretion of α-syn was no longer stimulated by the palmitoylation deficient DNAJC5 XP-L115R monomer.
source: Correspondingly, secretion of α-syn was no longer stimulated by the palmitoylation deficient DNAJC5 XP-L115R monomer (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the secretion assay shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Punctate DNAJC5 XP-L115R was widely associated with enlarged endosomes.
source: In contrast to the diffuse distribution of the DNAJC5 L115R mutant, which was excluded from the interior of enlarged endosomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), punctate DNAJC5 XP-L115R was widely associated with enlarged endosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Internalization events of DNAJC5 XP-L115R were found in several enlarged endosomes.
source: Internalization events were found in several enlarged endosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, magnified insets).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: mNG-α-syn was incorporated into endosomal compartments in cells coexpressing DNAJC5 XP-L115R.
source: mNG-α-syn was also incorporated into endosomal compartments in cells coexpressing DNAJC5 XP-L115R (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The level of α-syn-containing endosomes in cells expressing DNAJC5 XP-L115R was ~2-fold higher than in cells expressing the DNAJC5 L115R mutant.
source: The level of α-syn-containing endosomes in cells expressing DNAJC5 XP-L115R was ~2-fold higher than in cells expressing the DNAJC5 L115R mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Imaging data corroborate the biochemical similarity between WT DNAJC5 and DNAJC5 XP-L115R.
source: Our imaging data corroborate the biochemical similarity between WT DNAJC5 and DNAJC5 XP-L115R.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging and biochemical experiments.

claim: SH-SY5Y is a neuroblastoma line that differentiates in the presence of retinoic acid (RA) into nerve cells that express dopamine neuron (DA) markers including tyrosine hydroxylase (TH).
source: To evaluate the function of DNAJC5 in α-syn secretion at physiological levels of expression in a neuronal cell line, we employed SH-SY5Y, a neuroblastoma line that differentiates in the presence of retinoic acid (RA) into nerve cells that express dopamine neuron (DA) markers including tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) (Lopes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Elevated levels of expression of α-syn and dopamine transporter (DAT) were observed in SH-SY5Y cells after 6 days of RA-induced differentiation.
source: We observed elevated levels of expression of α-syn and dopamine transporter (DAT) in SH-SY5Y cells after 6 days of RA-induced differentiation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Fractionation of SH-SY5Y cell lysates resolved DNAJC5 into the low electrophoretic mobility P form associated with sedimentable membranes (M) and the non-sedimentable cytosolic NP form.
source: Fractionation of SH-SY5Y cell lysates resolved DNAJC5 into the low electrophoretic mobility P form associated with sedimentable membranes (M) and the non-sedimentable cytosolic NP form (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the fractionation experiment shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Hydroxylamine treatment of the membrane-associated form of DNAJC5 converted it to the electrophoretic mobility position of the NP form.
source: Hydroxylamine treatment of the membrane-associated form converted DNAJC5 to the electrophoretic mobility position of the NP form, as before (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the depalmitoylation experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: About 300 pg/ml α-syn was detected secreted into the supernatant of RA-differentiated SH-SY5Y cells using a sensitive α-syn ELISA.
source: We employed a sensitive α-syn enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and detected about 300 pg/ml α-syn secreted into the supernatant of RA-differentiated SH-SY5Y cells (Førland et al., 2018; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the ELISA experiment shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Differential centrifugation of the medium fraction demonstrated that the bulk of the secreted α-syn remained soluble.
source: Differential centrifugation of the medium fraction demonstrated that the bulk of the secreted α-syn remained soluble (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the medium fractionation experiment shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Flot-2 and DNAJC5 in a 100k pellet fraction were resistant to degradation by proteinase K in the absence but not in the presence of TX-100, suggesting that both were protected within the lumen of EVs.
source: A 100k pellet fraction was probed by protease protection for the localization of Flot-2, an exosome marker and DNAJC5. Both were resistant to degradation by proteinase K in the absence but not in the presence of TX-100, suggesting that both were protected within the lumen of EVs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the protease protection assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Residual full-length (FL) α-syn in the pellet fraction was cleaved by proteinase K without or with detergent.
source: In contrast, residual full-length (FL) α-syn in the pellet fraction was cleaved by proteinase K without or with detergent (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the protease protection assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: α-syn secreted by differentiated SH-SY5Y cells was not buoyant whereas DNAJC5 appeared associated with membranes fractionating at the position of EVs in a sucrose gradient flotation.
source: As an additional test, sucrose gradient flotation of the high-speed pellet fraction as used in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A revealed that α-syn secreted by differentiated SH-SY5Y cells was not buoyant whereas DNAJC5 appeared associated with membranes fractionating at the position of EVs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the sucrose gradient flotation experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: α-syn secreted by differentiated SH-SY5Y cells appears not to be enclosed within EVs.
source: Thus, as with HEK293T cells, α-syn secreted by differentiated SH-SY5Y cells appears not to be enclosed within EVs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fractionation and flotation experiments.

claim: Midbrain dopamine (mDA) neurons differentiated from human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) from Parkinson's patients with the GBA-N370S mutation release about twice the level of α-syn compared to control WT neurons.
source: Midbrain dopamine (mDA) neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) differentiated from human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) from Parkinson's patients with the GBA-N370S mutation, a genetic lesion that causes ER stress and dysfunctional lysosomes, release about twice the level of α-syn compared to control WT neurons (Fernandes et al., 2016; Lang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Treatment of GBAN370S hiPSC-derived dopamine neurons with the DNAJC5 inhibitor quercetin led to a significant dose-dependent reduction in the secretion of endogenous α-syn.
source: Treatment of GBAN370S hiPSC-derived dopamine neurons with the DNAJC5 inhibitor quercetin led to a significant dose-dependent reduction in the secretion of endogenous α-syn (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Endogenous DNAJC5 in hiPSC-derived dopamine neurons is natively palmitoylated which can be partially reduced by treatment with 2-BA (10 μM).
source: Immunoblotting of hiPSC-derived dopamine neuron lysate revealed that the endogenous DNAJC5 is natively palmitoylated which can be partially reduced by treatment with 2-BA (10 μM) to induce the formation of the lower, non-palmitoylated band (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Partial de-palmitoylation of DNAJC5 by 2-BA was insufficient to inhibit α-syn release by iPSC-derived GBA-N370S dopamine neurons at the concentration of 2-BA used.
source: However, this partial de-palmitoylation of DNAJC5 was insufficient to inhibit α-syn release by iPSC-derived GBA-N370S dopamine neurons at the concentration of 2-BA used (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: DNAJC5 was successfully depleted in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells by shRNA transduction.
source: The efficiency of shRNA targeting DNAJC5 was confirmed by knockdown (KD) of endogenous DNAJC5 in HEK293T cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A). Similarly, DNAJC5 was successfully depleted in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Secretion of α-syn was reduced fivefold in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells depleted of DNAJC5 compared with a control transduced with shRNA targeting GFP.
source: As a result, secretion of α-syn was reduced fivefold compared with a control transduced with shRNA targeting GFP (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Analysis of conditioned media by ELISA revealed a twofold elevated α-syn secretion in DNAJC5 WT overexpressing mDA compared to control with an empty vector in the presence of BaFA1.
source: Analysis of conditioned media by ELISA revealed a twofold elevated α-syn secretion in DNAJC5 WT overexpressing mDA compared to control with an empty vector in the presence of BaFA1 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the ELISA experiment shown in Figure 7E.

claim: With both BaFA1 treatment and DNAJC5 overexpression, α-syn secretion was increased threefold.
source: With both BaFA1 treatment and DNAJC5 overexpression, α-syn secretion was increased threefold (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the ELISA experiment shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The effect of BaFA1 inhibition was indicated by the appearance of a lipidated form of LC3 (LC3-II).
source: We examined the cell lysate of mDA by immunoblot. The effect of BaFA1 inhibition was indicated by the appearance of a lipidated form of LC3 (LC3-II) (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunoblot shown in Figure 7F.

claim: BaFA1 treatment induced more DNAJC5 oligomer formation.
source: BaFA1 treatment also induced more DNAJC5 oligomer formation (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunoblot shown in Figure 7F.

claim: DNAJC5 stimulates α-syn secretion in differentiated DA neurons as it does in HEK293T cells.
source: We conclude that DNAJC5 stimulates α-syn secretion in differentiated DA neurons as it does in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in differentiated neurons.

claim: The structure of the J domain of DNAJC5 has been solved by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR).
source: The structure of the J domain of DNAJC5 has been solved by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) (Patel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Recent progress in deep learning algorithms, exemplified by AlphaFold, enables atomic accuracy in protein structure prediction.
source: Recent progress in deep learning algorithms, exemplified by AlphaFold, enables atomic accuracy in protein structure prediction (Jumper et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the predicted structure of FL DNAJC5, the J domain showed a conserved overall globular J protein fold within the N-terminus, linked by the helical CS domain to the flexible C-terminal tail.
source: In the predicted structure, the J domain showed a conserved overall globular J protein fold within the N-terminus, linked by the helical CS domain to the flexible C-terminal tail.
evidence: This is based on the AlphaFold prediction shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Only a short helix was predicted to reside within the C-tail of DNAJC5.
source: Only a short helix was predicted to reside within the C-tail (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on the AlphaFold prediction shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Oligomerization of DNAJC5 increased when the J domain was deleted.
source: Using this information, we showed that oligomerization of DNAJC5 increased when the J domain was deleted (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Figure 8C.

claim: Deletion of the J domain increased the level of α-syn secretion induced by DNAJC5.
source: As recently reported by Lee et al., 2022, deletion of the J domain increased the level of α-syn secretion induced by DNAJC5 (Figure 8B and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 8B and D, and supported by citation.

claim: All four DNAJC5 C-terminal truncations were expressed and formed oligomers in cells.
source: All four DNAJC5 C-terminal truncations were expressed and formed oligomers in cells (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 8F.

claim: C-terminal truncated oligomers of DNAJC5 were co-secreted with α-syn into the medium.
source: C-terminal truncated oligomers were co-secreted with α-syn into the medium (Figure 8E and G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 8E and G.

claim: Neither the J domain nor the C-tail is required for DNAJC5 to induce α-syn secretion.
source: This result demonstrates that neither the J domain nor the C-tail is required for DNAJC5 to induce α-syn secretion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments with J domain deletion and C-terminal truncations.

claim: Transmission of protein aggregates and subsequent self-amplification is emerging as a common theme across various neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Transmission of protein aggregates and subsequent self-amplification is emerging as a common theme across various neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field, supported by the literature.

claim: DNAJC5-regulated α-syn secretion was reconstituted in cultured HEK293T cells, in RA neuronally differentiated human cells and in hiPSC-derived midbrain DA neurons.
source: In this study, we reconstituted DNAJC5-regulated α-syn secretion in cultured HEK293T cells, in RA neuronally differentiated human cells and in hiPSC-derived midbrain DA neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental systems used in the study.

claim: Membrane-anchoring of DNAJC5 through palmitoylation is crucial for its secretion and the secretion of α-syn as a soluble monomer.
source: By combining this assay with medium and cellular fractionation, we demonstrated that membrane-anchoring of DNAJC5 through palmitoylation is crucial for its secretion and the secretion of α-syn as a soluble monomer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fractionation and palmitoylation experiments.

claim: The topological locations of DNAJC5 and α-syn within enlarged endosomes were observed, presumably at an intermediate stage prior to secretion.
source: In addition, we observed the topological locations of DNAJC5 and α-syn within enlarged endosomes, presumably at an intermediate stage prior to secretion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging experiments.

claim: The findings on the role of DNAJC5 extend to differentiated DA neurons of human and mouse origin.
source: Our findings on the role of DNAJC5 extend to differentiated DA neurons of human and mouse origin.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings in neuronal systems.

claim: Both palmitoylation and oligomerization are solely dependent on the CS domain, which is required for α-syn secretion.
source: Finally, we provide evidence that both palmitoylation and oligomerization are solely dependent on the CS domain, which is required for α-syn secretion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the domain deletion and mutation experiments.

claim: Palmitoylated DNAJC5 oligomers function at a step involving membrane translocation of cytosolic α-syn, enabling it to become competent for secretion.
source: Based on our biochemical assays and imaging observations, we propose that palmitoylated DNAJC5 oligomers function at a step involving membrane translocation of cytosolic α-syn, enabling it to become competent for secretion (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings, illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: The in vivo toxicity of α-syn aggregates remains elusive.
source: The in vivo toxicity of α-syn aggregates remains elusive (Lashuel et al., 2013), but its propagation accompanies the progression of PD (Braak et al., 2006; Braak et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: α-syn propagation accompanies the progression of PD.
source: The in vivo toxicity of α-syn aggregates remains elusive (Lashuel et al., 2013), but its propagation accompanies the progression of PD (Braak et al., 2006; Braak et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on PD progression.

claim: DNAJC5 expression decreases in α-syn transgenic mice.
source: Recently, Caló et al., 2021 found that DNAJC5 expression decreases in α-syn transgenic mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Overexpression of DNAJC5 in vivo is reported to rescue α-syn aggregation-dependent pathology and increase the accumulation of monomeric α-syn.
source: Overexpression of DNAJC5 in vivo is reported to rescue α-syn aggregation-dependent pathology and increase the accumulation of monomeric α-syn (Caló et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: iPSC-derived neurons secrete α-syn in a largely soluble form.
source: As we find and others have reported, iPSC-derived neurons also secrete α-syn in a largely soluble form (Fernandes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation and the experimental findings in the study.

claim: α-syn is secreted in culture cells as a soluble monomeric species not enclosed within EVs, regardless of mutations modeled on PD or as expressed in tandem arrays or in gene fusions to tightly folded proteins.
source: Using the criteria of differential sedimentation and gel filtration chromatography, we conclude that α-syn is secreted in cultures cells as a soluble monomeric species not enclosed within EVs, regardless of mutations modeled on PD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) or as expressed in tandem arrays or in gene fusions to tightly folded proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the medium fractionation and gel filtration experiments.

claim: Other MAPS substrates are reported to be secreted in a soluble form.
source: Consistent with our results, other MAPS substrates are also reported to be secreted in a soluble form (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: α-syn oligomers have been found in EVs.
source: Although α-syn oligomers have also been found in EVs (Danzer et al., 2012; Emmanouilidou et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2020), we see no evidence for this in our culture medium fractionation and immunoblot experiments (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies, but the authors note they did not observe this in their experiments.

claim: 85% of secreted α-syn was found to be soluble using a Nluc assay.
source: With a more sensitive and quantitative Nluc assay, 85% of secreted α-syn was found to be soluble (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the Nluc assay shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The basal level of α-syn secreted by differentiated neuroblastoma cells is mainly soluble and not detected within EVs.
source: Similarly, the basal level of α-syn secreted by differentiated neuroblastoma cells is mainly soluble and not detected within EVs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The release of soluble α-syn may be an early event in pathogenesis of PD, prior to the deposition of aggregates.
source: The release of soluble α-syn may be an early event in pathogenesis of PD, prior to the deposition of aggregates.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings.

claim: Inhibition of the lysosomal ATPase with bafilomycin A (BaFA1) is known to induce lysosome fusion to the cell surface and secretion of lysosomal content including both soluble and aggregate forms of α-syn.
source: Inhibition of the lysosomal ATPase with bafilomycin A (BaFA1) is known to induce lysosome fusion to the cell surface and secretion of lysosomal content including both soluble and aggregate forms of α-syn (Xie et al., 2022; Figure 1—figure supplement 3H, Figure 7E).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and shown in the experiments.

claim: Such secretion may be part of a cell protective mechanism but it may also promote the interneuronal spread of monomer and oligomer.
source: Such secretion may be part of a cell protective mechanism but it may also promote the interneuronal spread of monomer and oligomer.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential roles of α-syn secretion.

claim: Numerous neuronal proteins are palmitoylated, including synaptic scaffolding proteins, signaling proteins, and synaptic vesicle proteins.
source: Numerous neuronal proteins are palmitoylated, including synaptic scaffolding proteins, signaling proteins, and synaptic vesicle proteins (Linder and Deschenes, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Protein palmitoylation has been implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Protein palmitoylation has been implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases (Cho and Park, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In PD, a recent study reported that upregulation of cellular palmitoylation decreased α-syn cytoplasmic inclusions.
source: In PD particularly, a recent study reported that upregulation of cellular palmitoylation decreased α-syn cytoplasmic inclusions (Ho et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The neuropathology and behavior deficiency of Huntington disease (HD) mice can be reversed by boosting brain palmitoylation.
source: The neuropathology and behavior deficiency of Huntington disease (HD) mice can be reversed by boosting brain palmitoylation (Virlogeux et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The secretion of neurodegenerative disease proteins is dependent on palmitoylation, possibly alleviating the cellular burden of protein aggregate accumulation.
source: Our results suggested that the secretion of neurodegenerative disease proteins is also dependent on palmitoylation, possibly alleviating the cellular burden of protein aggregate accumulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the palmitoylation experiments, with a speculative component.

claim: The general inhibition of cellular palmitoylation by 2-BA led to a complete block of α-syn secretion, whereas the specific palmitoylation deficient DNAJC5 mutant L115R only partially decreased α-syn secretion.
source: Notably, the general inhibition of cellular palmitoylation by 2-BA led to a complete block of α-syn secretion, whereas the specific palmitoylation deficient DNAJC5 mutant L115R only partially decreased α-syn secretion (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The difference between 2-BA and L115R effects implies the existence of palmitoylation-dependent factors other than DNAJC5.
source: The difference implies the existence of palmitoylation-dependent factors other than DNAJC5.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the difference in effects between 2-BA and L115R.

claim: EV-associated P-DNAJC5 clearly separated from soluble α-syn in the culture medium.
source: Although DNAJC5 coexpressed with α-syn and palmitoylation are required for secretion, EV-associated P-DNAJC5 clearly separated from soluble α-syn in the culture medium (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the medium fractionation experiments.

claim: The internalized DNAJC5 inside enlarged endosomes had both punctate and diffuse distributions, which may represent the soluble NP-DNAJC5 and membrane-attached P-DNAJC5, respectively.
source: In our live-cell imaging experiments, the internalized DNAJC5 inside enlarged endosomes had both punctate and diffuse distributions (Figure 4A). This may represent the soluble NP-DNAJC5 and membrane-attached P-DNAJC5, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiment with a speculative interpretation.

claim: The separation of DNAJC5 and α-syn may occur prior to their secretion when the late endosome and plasma membrane fuse.
source: In the time-lapse imaging of internalized α-syn induced by DNAJC5, both DNAJC5 and α-syn moved dynamically inside the compartment, without significant colocalization (Figure 4—video 1). This observation suggests that the separation of DNAJC5 and α-syn may occur prior to their secretion when the late endosome and plasma membrane fuse.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the imaging observations.

claim: Zhang et al., 2020 have reported a novel membrane channel, TMED10, for the unconventional secretion of IL-1β.
source: Zhang et al., 2020 have reported a novel membrane channel, TMED10, for the unconventional secretion of IL-1β.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Zhang et al. speculate an activation-on-demand oligomerization of TMED10 membrane subunits to form a conducting channel for substrate translocation, a process they refer to as THU.
source: These authors speculate an activation-on-demand oligomerization of TMED10 membrane subunits to form a conducting channel for substrate translocation, a process they refer to as THU (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative model from a cited study.

claim: α-syn was reported to not depend on TMED10 for unconventional secretion.
source: α-syn was reported to not depend on TMED10 for unconventional secretion (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study.

claim: In chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), cytosolic substrates are proposed to be translocated into lysosomes through a channel formed by the oligomerization of a single-transmembrane protein, LAMP2A.
source: Similarly, in chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), cytosolic substrates are proposed to be translocated into lysosomes through a channel formed by the oligomerization of a single-transmembrane protein, LAMP2A (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The secretion of α-syn has been shown to be independent of CMA.
source: The secretion of α-syn has been shown to be independent of CMA (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study.

claim: Without a transmembrane domain, membrane-tethered P-DNAJC5 oligomer is unlikely to be a channel for translocation.
source: Without a transmembrane domain, membrane-tethered P-DNAJC5 oligomer is unlikely to be a channel for translocation.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the structure of DNAJC5.

claim: A recent report identified CD98hc, an AA transporter subunit, to be a DNAJC5 interactor that is required for α-syn secretion.
source: A recent report identified CD98hc, an AA transporter subunit, to be a DNAJC5 interactor that is required for α-syn secretion (Lee et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: It remains to be determined whether CD98hc or other as yet uncharacterized membrane proteins are directly involved in α-syn membrane translocation.
source: It remains to be determined whether CD98hc or other as yet uncharacterized membrane proteins are directly involved in α-syn membrane translocation.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.
